entries.test: Public venture funding totals, OpenAI's round size, financial results and projections, and contemporary product comparisons would test these assertions.
entries.note: The passage is introduced as George Noble's reprinted analysis, not Marcus's own words. The normalization also softens the stated 65% to 'about 65%'.

entries.test: Public reliability studies, customer purchasing evidence, and financial reporting could establish whether unreliability limits willingness to pay and contributes to OpenAI's profitability difficulties.
entries.note: The source limits the willingness-to-pay claim to 'many people'; the normalization drops that scope restriction.

entries.test: OpenAI's publicly reported operating costs, revenues, and margins would show whether expensive operation contributes to its profitability difficulties.
entries.note: This faithfully extracts one of the three asserted causes.

entries.test: Public capability comparisons, competing product availability, pricing histories, and financial reporting could establish whether a lack of defensible technical advantages drove price competition and impaired profitability.
entries.note: Technical moat has a plain competitive meaning in this context.

entries.test: Contemporary public benchmarks, product capabilities, prices, and evidence of competitors reproducing OpenAI's advantages would test the claimed catch-up and its explanation.
entries.note: The phrase 'has also meant' asserts causation, not merely a comparison.

entries.test: Contemporary industry coverage from roughly 2024, reported OpenAI Code Red communications, and Google–OpenAI product comparisons as of publication would test the claim.
entries.note: The normalization replaces 'a couple years ago' with the unrestricted 'once', broadening the historical assertion.
The central assertion judges the valuation increase unjustified; its factual premises can be checked separately.
'A good chance' explicitly qualifies the prediction. 'Even with' describes supporting circumstances rather than a forecast antecedent.
In context, this expresses a negative judgment about the financing's financial justification.
